text: A stage magician's art lives in his hands, and Ethan has lost the use of his. What he asks the court for is not money or care but permission to stop, and the request becomes public property the moment it is filed. Sanjay Leela Bhansali films this as a romance, which is the unexpected decision: not a legal drama with feeling bolted on, but a love story with a petition at its centre. Two hours and six minutes leaves room for both, and most of the pressure falls on the ordinary business of a day — being lifted, being fed, being watched by people who hold opinions about a life they do not live in. The old trade sits underneath all of it. A man who spent his working years deciding exactly what an audience would be allowed to see is now the thing everyone is looking at, and the choosing has passed to a judge.

Morán did the arithmetic before anything else: $650,000, exactly double what the bank would pay him between today and his retirement. The theft is almost a footnote to the sum. What he wants is the time, and he has decided that a stretch in prison is a reasonable price for buying it outright — a proposal he puts to his colleague Román over dinner, in the tone of a business partnership. Three hours and ten minutes for a heist announces that Rodrigo Moreno is not much interested in heists. The film makes room for the clerk nobody at the Buenos Aires branch can quite see, for two names one letter apart, for the accumulated hours of a working life that films normally skip because nothing occurs in them. The comedy is dry and largely administrative. Crime here produces mostly waiting, which is what the job produced too.

Three people, one shared stretch of time, and two accounts of it that refuse to line up. Young-soo, who makes films, introduces Soo-jung, who writes, to his friend Jae-hoon, and the introduction does what introductions tend to do in a Hong Sang-soo film: it leaves everyone slightly worse off and a good deal more talkative. Then the material comes back around with its details rearranged. Nobody is lying, exactly. Each telling belongs to whoever is doing the remembering, and the gaps between them — an hour, a motive, who was waiting for whom — carry most of the film's wit. What is left after 127 minutes is not a solved discrepancy but a working model of how two people can spend the same evening and come away owning different versions of it, each certain the other has misremembered.

Every one of these rooms was arranged by the person who owns it, and then that person agreed to let a camera in. The double consent is what makes the film awkward rather than merely lurid: nothing has been caught, everything is being presented. Ulrich Seidl goes down the stairs of Austrian houses to the floor below the family floor, where a room can be fitted out for whatever the storeys above will not accommodate — a collection, an appetite, a ceremony with one participant. Eighty-one minutes, and the argument about national character never quite gets stated, though the invitation to make one is left lying about. What the film has instead is the patience of people showing a visitor their best thing. They stand in the middle of what they have built and wait to be looked at, and the looking runs a beat past where politeness would stop.

Korea prayed to whales once, and now it pours steel, and Kelvin Kyung Kun Park refuses to arrange those two facts into progress. The camera treats heavy industry the way it might treat a shrine — comparable scale, comparable submission demanded of a body, and no one standing inside it can see the whole animal at once. Ninety-eight minutes is a long time to hold a comparison open without letting it harden into a thesis, and the holding is what the film is for. The question it puts about the future is a real one, not a rhetorical device with the answer parked behind it. What comes instead of an argument is magnitude, and a suspicion that the old worship and the new industry ask the same thing of the people living among them.

She is a nurse and she is going west; he has lost his job as a security guard and he is going east. Neither exchange is fair, and both of them are betting otherwise. Ulrich Seidl gives the two journeys equal weight across 135 minutes, so the promise held out on one side of the border can be measured against the promise on the other in something close to real time. Work is the whole of the subject: what needs doing, who will pay for it, what a person will accept once the fare has been spent and going home is no longer a plan. Very little arrives as drama in the usual sense. Scenes run on, rooms are shown at length, and the discomfort that produces is not a side effect — it is the nearest thing the film has to a stated position.

Walter Sparrow catches stray dogs for the city, and then he reads a paperback that appears to know him. The resemblances pile up the way resemblances do once a man starts counting — a date, a name, a sum that folds down to the same two digits however it is added — and the film is candid about the mechanism, which is that anyone with a grievance and a pencil can prove whatever he needs to. Joel Schumacher takes the conceit at its word for 97 minutes and gives it a pulp finish, since the novel has to be pictured as well as read. It is sharpest early, when Walter is merely nettled: a man with a pen, underlining. Arithmetic as a hobby is comic. Arithmetic as an explanation for one's own life is a different condition, and the film knows when it crosses over.

The substitute's contract comes with an end date printed on it, and Henry Barthes has organised a life around that clause. Three weeks in one school, then another, then another: long enough to teach something, too short for anyone to start depending on him. Tony Kaye spreads the film across a group — administrators, teachers, students who can tell within a minute who is staying — and lets Henry narrate his way through, which is its own form of standing back. Ninety-eight minutes, and none of it is subtle; the film raises its voice and keeps it raised. What holds is the premise underneath, plain and hard to shake: a man can be very good with people precisely because he has already arranged not to be there next month.

A therapist decides to start writing again, and the first thing she reaches for is her newest patient's life. Margot is an actress in trouble, and trouble is usable; Sibyl keeps the sessions running and tells herself the two activities are separable. Justine Triet is exact about the permissions people grant themselves once the material is good — the appointment that runs long, the detail too useful to leave out, the note made afterwards — and exact about the speed at which a professional relationship turns into a supply line. Meanwhile Sibyl's own past starts coming up through the floor of the book. At 101 minutes the film changes register without warning and rarely settles, and there is no clean way to say whether the disorder belongs to Sibyl's life or to the novel she is assembling out of somebody else's.
